TimelineIndexAccessor::is_monotonic_decreasing¶

Back to Timeline Index Accessor API Reference

Signature¶

bool TimelineIndexAccessor::is_monotonic_decreasing() const

What The Predicate Proves¶

is_monotonic_decreasing() answers whether every timestamp is less than or equal to the timestamp before it. Equality is intentional: repeated instants do not break monotonicity. The predicate tests order only; use is_unique() when repeated instants are the concern.

This distinction matters when validating an externally supplied axis. A series of readings may be newest-first and still be well ordered, even though most ordered lookup and resampling operations require the opposite, increasing direction. This method lets a caller distinguish that deliberate reverse order from a genuinely scrambled axis without sorting or allocating another TimelineIndexAccessor.

The result is a native C++ bool, not a one-element container. Empty and single-element axes return true: neither contains an adjacent pair that violates decreasing order. The check compares stored epoch nanoseconds, so the timezone used to display those instants cannot change the answer.

Examples¶

Example 1. An ordinary increasing axis is not decreasing.

auto index = pluss::timeindex::make({
    "2024-11-01T00:00:00Z",
    "2024-11-01T00:20:00Z",
    "2024-11-01T00:40:00Z",
});

std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << index.is_monotonic_decreasing() << "\n";

Output¶

false

Example 2. Build a newest-first axis with construction-time order enforcement disabled, then validate its intended direction explicitly.

auto newest_first = pluss::timeindex::make({
    "2024-11-01T01:20:00Z",
    "2024-11-01T01:00:00Z",
    "2024-11-01T00:40:00Z",
    "2024-11-01T00:20:00Z",
    "2024-11-01T00:00:00Z",
}, false);

std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << newest_first.is_monotonic_decreasing() << "\n";

Output¶

true

Example 3. Equal neighbors satisfy both monotonic directions. They affect uniqueness, not ordering.

auto tied = pluss::timeindex::make({
    "2025-01-03T00:00:00Z",
    "2025-01-02T00:00:00Z",
    "2025-01-02T00:00:00Z",
    "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z",
}, false);

std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "decreasing=" << tied.is_monotonic_decreasing() << "\n"
          << "unique=" << tied.is_unique() << "\n";

Output¶

decreasing=true
unique=false

Example 4. Trivial axes are monotonically decreasing by definition.

auto one = pluss::timeindex::make("2025-01-01T00:00:00Z");
auto none = pluss::timeindex::make(std::vector<std::int64_t>{});

std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "one=" << one.is_monotonic_decreasing() << "\n"
          << "none=" << none.is_monotonic_decreasing() << "\n";

Output¶

one=true
none=true

Cost And Ownership¶

The method performs one forward scan and stops at the first increasing pair. Its worst-case cost is linear in the number of timestamps, its auxiliary space is constant, and it neither mutates nor copies the axis.

See Also¶

  • TimelineIndexAccessor::is_monotonic_increasing: validate the order required by ordered lookup and resampling.

  • TimelineIndexAccessor::is_unique: detect repeated instants independently of direction.

  • TimelineIndexAccessor::sort: produce an increasing axis when reordering is appropriate.
